headline: Gomakasu may come from 護摩 (goma, “a holy fire in esoteric Buddhism”) plus the suffix かす (kasu), or from 胡麻菓子 (goma kashi, “sesame candy”).
レントゲン is from German Röntgen.
Katte is 勝ち (kachi, “victory, win, advantage”) plus 手 (te, “means, way; hand”).
ヒント is borrowed from English hint and is first attested in 1886.
Ugoki is the continuative stem of the verb 動く (ugoku).
Aete is 敢え (ae, the stem of 敢ふ (afu, “to bear, endure”)) plus て (te, conjunctive suffix).
Kanroku originally referred to a samurai's pay, from 貫 (kan) plus 禄 (roku), the salary of someone in government service.
Omoitsuki is the continuative stem of the verb 思い付く (omoitsuku, “to think of”).
トラブル is borrowed from English trouble.
ナンセンス is from English nonsense.
In sanbi, 賛 is a daiyōji replacing 讃.
Chō, “super-”, is from Middle Chinese 超 (MC trhjew).
Aburae is 油 (abura, “oil”) plus 絵 (e, “picture”).
Okasu, “to perpetrate”, is a doublet of 冒す (okasu, “to risk”) and 侵す (okasu, “to invade; to infringe”).
Ikigai is 生きる (ikiru, “to live, to exist”) plus 甲斐 (kai, “worth, value”), with kai voiced to gai by rendaku.
Goi is 語 (go, “word”) plus 彙 (i, “collection”).
Kireme is 切れる (kireru, “to be cut, to become fissured”) plus 目 (me, “dividing point, border line”).
スター is borrowed from English star.
Rui, “kind”, is from Middle Chinese 類 (MC lwijH).
レッスン is borrowed from English lesson.
バット covers “bat” and “vat”, and the source borrows both from English.
Okonai is the continuative stem of the verb 行う (okonau).
Uchiwa is 打ち (uchi, “hitting; batting”) plus 羽 (wa, “wing”), and its kanji are an example of jukujikun.
Wazurawashii is from the verb 煩う (wazurau, “to worry about”).
Manmarui is from 真ん丸 (manmaru).
Tsuranuku is 列 (tsura, “row”, archaic) plus 抜く (nuku, “to go through”).
In renpō, 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.
Mudazukai is 無駄 (“futility, waste”) plus 遣い (“use, usage”).
Tejun is 手 (te, “means”) plus 順 (-jun, “order”).
Tenohira is 手 (te, “hand”) plus の (no) plus 平 (hira, “flat”), and the source compares English flat of one's hand.
